text: Lesson eleven gave us net returns. This lesson asks the harder question: what risk did it take to earn them, and how did SR-5 actually behave when markets broke?

Beyond Sharpe, Sortino of 0.58 only penalizes downside volatility, and Calmar of 0.27 scales return against the worst drawdown. On net daily returns across the full out-of-sample window, VaR at the 95 percent level is about negative 0.62 percent, with a CVaR of negative 0.95 percent; at the 99 percent level, VaR is about negative 1.15 percent and CVaR negative 1.6 percent. Beta to SPY normally sits near 0.04 — essentially no persistent market exposure, as a dollar-neutral book should have.

max_drawdown walks the equity curve's running peak and measures the worst peak-to-trough decline. Sharpe annualizes the mean-over-standard-deviation of daily returns. VaR95 is simply the 5th percentile of the daily return distribution, and CVaR95 averages everything worse than that cutoff — the part of the tail a single VaR number hides.

Four real windows test this directly. During the COVID crash, February 20th through March 23rd, 2020, SR-5 lost 6.1 percent while SPY fell 33.9 percent. In the Q4 2018 selloff, SR-5 gained 1.8 percent while SPY dropped 19.4 percent. Through the 2022 rate-hike bear market, SR-5 lost 3.4 percent against SPY's 24.5 percent decline. And in the August 2024 VIX spike, SR-5 gained 0.9 percent while SPY fell 6.0 percent.

But dollar-neutral doesn't mean immune. That near-zero 0.04 beta spikes to roughly 0.25 during the COVID crash specifically, because when every sector sells off together — the classic correlation-to-one effect — the long and short legs stop offsetting each other as cleanly. Dollar-neutral construction reduces market exposure most of the time, not all of the time.
The risk picture is now complete. Next, Lesson 13 writes all of this — hypothesis, model, signal, costs, and risk — into the performance report.
